extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and advanced students interested in algebraic-equation transformations, analytical geometry, and classical constructions
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and constructive procedures for transforming algebraic equations (depressing terms, eliminating groups of coefficients), variation-of-parameter analyses for lines/surfaces, and geometric constructions (conics, arc functions, rectification). Includes worked algorithms and geometric constructions with cautions and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive-multiplier transformation law
rubrics_metrics.description: At every new transformation the first of the multipliers previously employed is omitted, and the rest, each augmented by the new increment of the variable, retrograde one step: the new increment itself supplying the place of such multipliers as are still deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this general law when applying successive incremental transformations (analogue of factorial combinations). Track how previously used multipliers shift and how the new increment fills missing multipliers; applies also when zero-increments occur (see plural/increment note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Never omit marginal memoranda
rubrics_metrics.description: The marginal memoranda should never be omitted. They consist of the leading multipliers in the respective courses, with indices annexed, which decrease regularly till they become stationary at 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marginal memoranda record leading multipliers and indices and indicate (a) how often the entire multiplier is to be used (index) and (b) the distance back at which the increment was introduced (difference between index and n). Always keep these notes to avoid misapplication of successive transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plural expression for increments after zero-increments
rubrics_metrics.description: A plural expression is adopted to prevent any perplexity when a real increment succeeds one or more zero-increments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing increments in the transformation algorithm, use plural forms to avoid ambiguity in sequences containing zero-increments; this is a wording convention to prevent misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about symmetric formation in subsidiary equations
rubrics_metrics.description: In a solution of a cubic deprived of its second term the subsidiary quantity p has three pairs of values, each pair corresponding to a different value of z: hence the laws of symmetric formation do not apply to the coefficients of the subsidiary equation considered as an equation in z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume symmetric-coefficient identities (from the original equation) transfer straightforwardly to coefficients of subsidiary equations in the new variable; check multiplicity and pairing of roots/parameters first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify algebraical-solution cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Those cases in which the equations can be satisfied by λ = 0 and λ' = 1 are cases admitting algebraical solutions, i.e., solvable without recourse to the full theory of equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify problems: if substitution values reduce condition equations to trivial values (0,1) the solution is algebraical and simpler methods can be used. Seek such simplifying substitutions before invoking general theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume (v + p)^m form to destroy consecutive terms
rubrics_metrics.description: In seeking to destroy m2 consecutive terms of an equation (starting with the second term), it is better to assume a transformed equation in (v + p)^m, which can immediately be reduced to the required form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: (1) reduces number of equations of condition, and (2) simplifies the remaining conditions. When terms to be destroyed are not consecutive or when modifying them, apply slight alterations to the same method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide homogeneous function by M^n and form f(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let any function, homogeneous and of the ath degree with respect to the quantities A, A', ..., be divided by M^n, and denote by ratios which the Ay etc. bear to M; the function when so divided is represented by f(b). Then analyze f^?(b)=0 and reduce by completing squares and choosing auxiliary variables determined from quadratics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a systematic device to lower degrees: divide by a suitable power, express ratios, manipulate to obtain quadratics in chosen variables (z_i), and thereby reduce an equation of high degree to lower-degree components (e.g., to h1^2 + h2^2 = 0 and onward). Follow the algebraic completion and substitution steps as shown (introducing hi = ... etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative decomposition into simpler equations (parity method)
rubrics_metrics.description: When b is odd the function f^?(b) may be reduced to a simple equation containing (b + 1) disposable ratios; f^(b) = (h^)^ = 0 may be decomposed into (b − 1) equations h1^ + h2^ = 0, etc., enabling elimination of many ratios and ultimately reaching a simple final equation F(3b + 1) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parity (odd/even) to plan decomposition; decompose into paired quadratic-type relations, eliminate by choosing upper/lower signs to simplify, and iteratively eliminate variables to reach a final equation in one variable. Keep track of the number of terms and parity at each stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive elimination without raising degree beyond highest function dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: General theorem assertion: any number of such functions can be simultaneously made equal to zero without having to solve an equation of a degree higher than the highest dimension of those functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategize eliminations so that intermediate auxiliary equations do not exceed the maximum degree present among the target functions. This motivates the choice of transformations that limit introduced degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm to remove specific middle terms of general nth-degree equation
rubrics_metrics.description: To deprive the general equation of the nth degree of its second, third, and fourth terms, assume for v an expression consisting of a certain number of terms (e.g., 22 terms) and determine auxiliary variables so that condition equations reduce to lower-degree subsidiary equations; eliminate sequentially to obtain a final cubic (or intended degree) determining the primary substitution variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the outlined sequence: assume v expansion, write condition equations (e.g., (14),(15)), reduce those to f^(2)=0, eliminate between them to get f^(1)=0 (final cubic), then back-substitute. The choice of number of terms in v matches the number of terms you wish to cancel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound on dimensions used in elimination (example: ≤7 in many cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general the removal of a given set of terms may be done by means of equations whose dimensions do not exceed a certain bound (in an example given, 7); limitations to this proposition are noted to be considered subsequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning elimination, check the claimed maximal auxiliary degree relevant to your case. The bound may vary with the specific set of terms; consult subsequent extensions/limitations before assuming a universal bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use resolution of functions into sums of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The resolution of functions into the sums of powers will be found useful in other branches of science, and operations like those in paragraph 3 are rendered simple by means of a law to which the quantities successively added are subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, write functions as sums of powers to simplify manipulations and repeated-addition laws; this can simplify the algebra in multi-step transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-order line: effect of variable coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For the straight line ay + bx + c = 0, if (1) a is variable (b,c constants) then all lines represented cut the a-axis at the same point determined by setting y = 0; (2) b variable => all lines pass through same point on y-axis; (3) c variable (a,b constants) => all lines are parallel (same tangent angle independent of c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine the geometric locus when one coefficient varies, set the appropriate coordinate to zero (y=0 or x=0) to find invariant intercepts or compute slope expression to check independence from the variable coefficient. Use these quick tests to classify the family of lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order curve: variable coefficient produces common contact points or fixed intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: For the general conic ay^2 + bxy + cx^2 + dy + ex + f = 0: (1) if a is variable and others fixed, the locus is a family of curves touching each other in the same two points (real or imaginary) on the a-axis (i.e., common points and common tangents); (2) if b is variable, the family intersects each other in the same four points of the coordinate axes; (3) if c,d,e variable variously, families may be similar and similarly situated, concentric, or intersect in fixed axis points depending on which coefficient varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove contact or intersection behavior by evaluating traces (set x=0 or y=0) to find invariant roots and by computing tangent equations to show tangents are independent of the varying parameter. Distinguish cases by which coefficient is variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane (first-order surface): varying a coefficient gives families intersecting in fixed lines or parallel planes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a plane az + by + cx + d = 0: if a is variable (others constant) the family of planes cut the plane of yz in the same straight line (found by setting z=0); if b or c variable analogous results hold; if d variable the family consists of parallel planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find invariant intersection lines or parallelism, set the coordinate orthogonal to the variable coefficient to zero and examine resulting trace equation; constancy indicates invariant trace or fixed direction/parallelism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order surface: variation of coefficients and tangent-plane method
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quadric surface with general second-degree equation, if a coefficient (e.g., a) is variable the family of surfaces touch each other and the curve of contact is a conic in a coordinate plane; proof proceeds by deriving a common tangent plane equation and showing it is independent of the varying parameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the tangent-plane derivation: take two points on the surface, subtract equations to isolate differences, express line through the points parametrically, and derive the tangent-plane equation. Show independence from the variable coefficient to establish common tangency/curve of contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order surface: various fixed-intersection and similarity properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific cases: (4) variable b => surfaces intersect in the same six points (two on each coordinate axis); (5,6) variable other coefficients may yield the same six points; (7–9) varying certain coefficients yields similar and similarly situated surfaces intersecting in a fixed conic; (10) varying f produces similar, similarly situated, concentric surfaces (centres independent of f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine invariant intersection points by setting coordinate pairs to zero and checking independence from the varying coefficient; determine similarity/concentricity by checking which coefficients control size/orientation (if those remain fixed, similarity ensues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Godfray semicircumference approximation construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction to approximate the semicircumference: given circle center O and diameter DA, draw BOC perpendicular; make OC equal to the diameter, AK equal to double the diameter; join CE, set off EF equal to diameter, describe arc with centre A, set off DG from I to H, join FH, draw CK parallel to FH, make Ka equal OK, draw AM parallel to EC, set AR = AN and Rw = BM; then aw approximates the semi-circumference. Claimed accuracy: true to seven decimal places (example gives 3.14159261546).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the geometric steps exactly; expected advantage: shorter construction than Pioché's and very high accuracy (error about 18 inches for earth-radius circle). Also two other briefer constructions provided but less accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use triangle-similarity and sec/tan relations to derive arc-function identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive fundamental formulas of two arcs (e.g., expressions involving sin, cos, tan, sec) via constructing radii and tangents at junction point A, using similarity of triangles KOA and EDF and perpendicular DF from D to OE; obtain relations like sin(a + b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b and equivalent sec/tan identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct tangents and perpendiculars as in the figures, denote arcs by a and b and radius by 1, use triangle similarity to connect lengths and then translate those length relations into trigonometric identities; this geometric derivation is suitable for instruction and systematization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribing triangle in a conic with sides parallel to given lines (Proposition I)
rubrics_metrics.description: To inscribe in a conic a triangle whose sides are parallel to three given lines: find points D, E, F on the conic whose tangents are parallel respectively to the given triangle's sides AB, AC, BC; join D, E, F; through D draw chord DG parallel to EF', through E draw EH parallel to DF', through F draw FK parallel to DE; triangle GHK will be similar to ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct tangents at chosen points so they are parallel to the desired directions, then draw chords and parallels as described to form the inscribed triangle. Scholium: ensure the given triangle is not drawn with any side parallel to the transverse axis of a hyperbola or axis of a parabola (otherwise construction fails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Porism on equal segments in conics and its constructive composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a point E on a diameter GH (inside or outside a conic), one can find F on the same diameter (or extension) so that chords through F to points where any arbitrary line through E meets the curve cut off equal segments. Composition: in ellipse/hyperbola choose F on GH so that OF is third proportional to OK and OG; in parabola choose F so GF = GE; draw FT conjugate to GH, then construct chords and parallels as described to obtain equal segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the composition steps: locate F by proportional construction depending on the conic type, draw the conjugate FT, pick chord AC through E meeting FT in T, draw chords AD and BC from F to extremities, draw parallels through A, C, E to TF and intersect to produce the chord endpoints. Use harmonic division and conjugacy facts to verify equality of segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar/pole method endorsement and coordinate cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of poles and polars, particularly combined with Cartesian coordinate methods, is a powerful engine for establishing complicated relations between points and lines of the second order and between planes and surfaces of the second degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating relations in conics/quadrics use the polar theory together with coordinate geometry to simplify derivations; the method yields many otherwise hard-to-find results and organizes complicated relations efficiently.
